comparisons.peer_summary: Total loss-absorbing capacity (TLAC) consists of Tier 1 capital and eligible long-term debt issued directly by the Corporation, which must be maintained in excess of minimum requirements plus buffers to avoid restrictions on capital distributions and discretionary bonus payments.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and Bank of America define TLAC as including equity capital and eligible long-term debt. Goldman Sachs specifies that eligible long-term debt is unsecured debt with a remaining maturity of at least one year, while Bank of America similarly defines eligible long-term debt as unsecured debt with a remaining maturity of at least one year satisfying TLAC rule requirements. Additionally, both disclose that TLAC levels must be maintained in excess of minimum requirements plus buffers; Bank of America explicitly links this requirement to avoiding restrictions on capital distributions and bonuses, whereas Goldman Sachs defines the composition of external long-term debt including haircuts for debt due between one and two years, a detail not explicitly detailed in the cited Bank of America sentence but consistent with the broader TLAC framework context.

sentences.text: • TLAC includes common and preferred stock, and eligible long-term debt issued by Group Inc. Eligible long-term debt represents unsecured debt, which has a remaining maturity of at least one year and satisfies additional requirements.
• External long-term debt consists of eligible long-term debt subject to a haircut if it is due to be paid between one and two years.
Total loss-absorbing capacity (TLAC) consists of the Corporation's Tier 1 capital and eligible long-term debt issued directly by the Corporation.
Eligible long-term debt for TLAC ratios is comprised of unsecured debt that has a remaining maturity of at least one year and satisfies additional requirements as prescribed in the TLAC final rule.

As with the risk-based capital ratios and SLR, the Corporation is required to maintain TLAC ratios in excess of minimum requirements plus applicable buffers to avoid restrictions on capital distributions and discretionary bonus payments to executive officers.

comparisons.peer_topic: Federal Reserve TLAC and LTD requirements
comparisons.peer_summary: The Federal Reserve requires U.S. GSIB top-tier holding companies, including the Firm, to maintain minimum levels of external Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) and eligible long-term debt.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures address the regulatory requirement for Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) for U.S. G-SIB holding companies. Goldman Sachs defines the composition of TLAC (stock and eligible debt) and external long-term debt within its capital management section. JPMorgan explicitly states the Federal Reserve's TLAC rule requirement for its top-tier holding company to maintain minimum levels of external TLAC and eligible long-term debt. While Goldman Sachs details the mechanical definition of eligible debt, JPMorgan cites the regulatory mandate itself, but both confirm the applicability of TLAC rules to the holding company level.

comparisons.peer_topic: TLAC and LTD Ratio Definitions and Requirements
comparisons.peer_summary: Required TLAC ratios include applicable buffers and consist of CET1 capital, Additional Tier 1 capital (excluding noncontrolling interests), and eligible LTD, with LTD reduced by 50% for unpaid principal due in one to two years. Clean holding company requirements prohibit covered BHCs from incurring external debt with maturities less than one year and cap certain other external liabilities at 5% of outstanding external TLAC, while capital deductions apply for investments in unsecured debt instruments issued by the Parent Company or other G-SIBs.
comparisons.comparison: Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley both define the components of external TLAC and the treatment of eligible long-term debt. Goldman Sachs states TLAC includes common and preferred stock and eligible long-term debt, with external long-term debt subject to a haircut if due between one and two years. Morgan Stanley similarly defines external TLAC as consisting of CET1 capital, Additional Tier 1 capital, and eligible LTD, and explicitly notes that eligible LTD is reduced by 50% for unpaid principal due in more than one but less than two years. Both disclosures highlight the specific reduction/haircut mechanism for debt in the 1-2 year maturity band as part of the TLAC calculation.
